newsitem.title: SENEGAL: Senegal marks Senghor's 90th birthday without him.
newsitem.headline: Senegal marks Senghor's 90th birthday without him.

text.p: Senegal's political family made a pilgrimage to the home town of its independence president Leopold Sedar Senghor on Wednesday to celebrate the 90th birthday of one of Africa's outstanding statesman.

But the frail poet-president, who in 1980 became the first modern African leader to quit the political stage voluntarily and now rarely appears in public, was absent from the party -- spending the day in his adopted country France.
President Abdou Diouf, the man who succeeded Senghor, led the celebration in Joal, a humble town despite its illustrious first son -- but smartened up for the occasion.

"Senghor is of the race of empire builders, a pathfinder, a guide who takes you by the hand to lead you up high on to the mountain," Diouf told assembled dignitaries and members of Senghor's family led by his nephew Adrien, a former government minister.
"This child of Joal and of Africa, whom they call Senghor in far away places, is a citizen of the world," he added.
Diouf said that henceforth Senegal's main airport and its biggest soccer stadium, both in the capital Dakar, would carry the name Leopold Senghor.
Moslem and Christian religious leaders also made the journey Joal, 130 km west of Dakar, after organising or attending a celebratory mass in the capital on Tuesday.
Senghor, a Christian who led the mainly Moslem former French colony for two decades, was once-decribed as the ideal philospher-ruler envisaged by ancient Greek philosopher Plato.

The first black man elected to France's prestigious Academie Francaise, he celebrated Negritude, a forerunner of the "black is beautiful" concept highlighting the role of the black races in the development of world culture.
Without Negro Africans, civilisation would "lack the rhythm section of its orchestra, the bass voice of its choir," he once said.

Short, softly spoken, Senghor, a former member of France's national assembly, played a key role in persuading President Charles de Gaulle that France's territories in black Africa could be fully independent inside the French community without serious risk of its dissolution.

A shrewd politician and a founder member of the Senegal's ruling Socialist Party, he emerged as president of an independent Senegal in 1960. He stayed in power with the backing of Senegal's two influential Moslem brotherhoods.
